Overall, Shelfmark is a strong early-stage concept with a real, well-documented problem, a coherent solution, and unusually credible early validation for a student team. Weaknesses lie mainly in the depth of differentiation and in unproven outcome claims, not in the underlying idea.

Problem and need: The pain point is real, specific, and grounded in established education research (summer learning loss concentrated among low-income children, compounding over years). The team goes beyond citing literature by surveying 120 parents in the pilot neighborhood: 83% wanted help, only 14% had found an affordable, walkable option. That gap between demand and accessible supply is a clear, quantified signal. The problem is also framed correctly as an access issue rather than an ability issue, and the critique of existing solutions (mismatched books in library programs, high-priced suburban chains, volunteer churn with no measurement) is logical and plausible.

Solution quality and uniqueness: The offering addresses the need in a compelling, integrated way. The combination of a trusted physical location (solving the supervision, device, and motivation gaps that undermine apps), fine-grained diagnostic-driven book matching (solving the too-hard-book-and-quit problem), and data-informed tutor pairing is thoughtful and ties directly to the stated failure modes of alternatives. Interest-weighted book selection is a smart engagement lever. The pricing, a sliding scale averaging $9 per session, is aligned with the target customers' ability to pay and is far below the $40-70 per hour chains, which makes the value proposition credible.

Evidence of traction: The pilot materially strengthens the concept: 74 children, $21,300 revenue, a $12,000 school contract, 91% attending at least 12 of 16 sessions, 4.7/5 satisfaction, and center-level break-even by week six. High attendance is a notable signal of genuine pull in a population where program dropout is typical.

Caveats and risks to the concept's strength: (1) Uniqueness is moderate rather than strong. Individual components (adaptive reading diagnostics, level-matched book lists, neighborhood tutoring) exist separately in the market, e.g., Lexile-based tools and nonprofit tutoring models. The claim that no one combines all three is plausible but unverified, and the combination is more an execution advantage than a hard-to-copy innovation. (2) The data moat is asserted rather than demonstrated; with one pilot of 74 children, the dataset is too small to support meaningful matching superiority, and it is unclear whether tutor-child matching improves outcomes over simple level-matched books plus any competent tutor. (3) The headline outcome (0.4 grade level gain) comes from an uncontrolled pilot with no comparison group and appears to rely on internal assessment using the team's own diagnostic; the comparison to 'typical loss' is not a true counterfactual. The planned independent evaluation is the right remedy but is not yet done. (4) The pilot sample of 61 paying or district-sponsored families out of 74 suggests some self-selection toward more engaged households, which may overstate how well the model works for the hardest-to-reach children. (5) The model is labor- and location-intensive, which is good for trust but makes the concept harder to scale than the software-centric framing suggests.

Verdict: A clearly identified, important problem; a logical, human-centered solution that fits the target population's constraints; and promising early evidence. The concept's main gaps are defensibility and rigorously proven impact. As a business idea it is above average in clarity and need-validation, with differentiation that rests on integrated execution rather than proprietary technology.

Business plan text:

Shelfmark
Shelfmark: Executive Summary
Problem
Every summer, children in low-income neighborhoods lose reading ground that their wealthier
peers do not. Decades of education research show that students from lower-income households can
lose roughly two to three months of reading achievement over the summer, while higher-income
students hold steady or gain slightly. Because the loss compounds year after year, by middle
school the gap can amount to years of reading skill. The gap is not a matter of ability. It
reflects access: fewer books at home, fewer enrichment programs nearby, and parents working
long hours who cannot supervise reading.
Existing fixes fall short. Public library summer programs are valuable but are rarely matched
to an individual child's level, so many children pick books that are too hard, get frustrated,
and quit. Large tutoring chains are expensive and located in wealthier suburbs. Free volunteer
programs struggle with tutor turnover and have no way to measure whether a child is improving.
In our pilot neighborhood, we surveyed 120 parents and found that 83 percent wanted summer
reading help for their child, but only 14 percent had found any program they could afford and
reach on foot.
Solution
Shelfmark is a neighborhood tutoring center that combines a physical, welcoming space with
reading-level analytics. When a child enrolls, they complete a fifteen-minute adaptive
diagnostic that places them on a fine-grained reading scale. Our matching engine then does two
things. First, it builds a personal shelf of books that sit in the child's productive range:
hard enough to grow, easy enough to enjoy. The engine also weighs the child's stated interests,
so a ten-year-old who loves soccer gets sports stories at the right level. Second, it pairs the
child with a tutor whose track record and teaching style fit the child's particular profile,
such as decoding difficulty versus comprehension difficulty.
After each session, the tutor logs a two-minute check, and the software updates the child's
level and adjusts the shelf. Parents receive a plain-language progress note. Centers are small
rented storefronts near schools and transit lines, staffed by trained local tutors, many of
them community college students and retired teachers. The physical presence matters: it gives
families a trusted place close to home, and it gives children a reason to show up.
Market
In the United States there are roughly 17 million children ages 8 to 12, and about one in five
lives in a household below the federal poverty line. Our initial target is the subset attending
Title I schools, approximately 3.5 million children nationally. Within our home metro area
alone, 41 Title I elementary and middle schools serve about 19,000 children in our age range.
If we reach 5 percent of them, that is roughly 950 students per summer from one metro area.
School districts are a second buyer. Districts receive federal and state funds earmarked for
summer learning and learning recovery, and they actively seek vendors who can show measured
outcomes. Our third market is other literacy programs, such as libraries and nonprofits, that
want our matching software without running a center. We estimate the combined serviceable
market in our first three metro areas at about 24 million dollars per year.
Business Model
We earn revenue from three streams. The first is family fees on a sliding scale from 0 to 18
dollars per session, with an average realized fee of 9 dollars. The second is district summer
contracts, priced at 410 dollars per enrolled student for an eight-week program, which covers
tutor pay, books, and software. The third is software licensing at 6 dollars per student seat
per month to outside programs.

Our pilot center, with a monthly rent of 2,100 dollars and a paid staff of one site lead and
six part-time tutors, reached center-level break-even in its sixth week. At 74 students, unit
economics showed a contribution margin of about 31 percent after tutor pay, books, and rent. We
expect margin to rise toward 40 percent as the matching engine lets each tutor handle more
students per hour and as book shelves are reused across cohorts.
Competition
Our competitors fall into three groups. National tutoring chains offer individualized help but
charge 40 to 70 dollars per hour and rarely locate in low-income districts. Digital reading
apps are cheap and scalable, but they depend on a child having a device, a quiet room, and
self-discipline, which our families often lack, and they provide no human relationship. Library
and nonprofit programs are free and trusted, but they offer limited personalization and little
outcome data.
Shelfmark's difference is the combination: a physical neighborhood presence, tutors matched by
data, and book matching based on a precise reading level. We know of no program that does all
three at a price families in our neighborhoods can pay. Our defensibility grows with data:
every session improves our matching model, and a larger dataset of child-tutor-book pairings is
hard for a newcomer to replicate.
Team
Maribel Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive, is a senior studying education policy and spent two
summers coordinating a library reading program. Tobias Lindqvist-Hart, chief technology
officer, is a computer science senior who built the matching engine and diagnostic. Priyanka
Venkataraghavan, head of curriculum, is a graduate student in literacy education and a former
elementary teacher who designed our tutor training. Dwayne Castellano, head of operations,
studies business and previously managed a community center, where he built relationships with
the school principals who referred our first families. All four of us are based at our
university and work on Shelfmark more than thirty hours a week.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the core concept, built a working prototype of the diagnostic and matching
software, and incorporated Shelfmark as a Delaware C Corporation with equal founder equity. Our
website is live and handles enrollment. Over one eight-week summer we ran a pilot center
serving 74 children, 61 of whom were paying families or district-sponsored. The pilot generated
21,300 dollars in revenue, including a 12,000 dollar contract with one elementary school. The
average child gained 0.4 grade levels in reading over the summer, compared with the typical
loss of a few months, and 91 percent of enrolled children attended at least 12 of 16 sessions.
Parent satisfaction averaged 4.7 out of 5.
Our plan for the next twelve months is to open three new centers in time for the coming summer,
serve about 550 students, and reach roughly 118,000 dollars in revenue. We project center-level
profitability at all sites and company-wide break-even in the second year as software licensing
grows.
What We Ask For
We are seeking 85,000 dollars in prize money or seed funding. About 45,000 dollars would fund
the three new centers, covering deposits, first-quarter rent, book collections, and tutor
training. About 25,000 dollars would extend the software to support more levels and a parent
dashboard. The remaining 15,000 dollars would cover legal, insurance, and an independent
evaluation of student outcomes, which we believe is the key to winning district contracts.
Beyond funding, we would value introductions to school district officials and mentors who have
scaled local service businesses.
